Online Reputation for Lawyers and Law Firms in Italy

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Online reputation for lawyers in Italy is shaped by a constraint most businesses do not have: the Code of Conduct of the Italian Bar (Codice deontologico forense) limits what a lawyer may say about clients, cases and their own results. A law firm can still build a strong search presence and handle negative reviews, but every reply and every piece of promotion has to respect professional secrecy, truthful information and the ban on soliciting clients.

Why search results matter so much for a law firm

Legal clients search before they call, and they search names rather than services. Someone facing a criminal charge in Rome or a family dispute in Milan usually receives two or three names from friends or colleagues and then compares what Google shows for each lawyer. The firm's site, the Google Business Profile with its rating, news mentions and any complaint posts become the shortlist filter.

The stakes are higher than in retail because the relationship is based on trust and discretion. A single result suggesting a disciplinary problem, a hostile post by an opposing party or a poor rating can decide the choice before any consultation takes place. For partners of larger firms, the personal name and the firm name carry separate risks: a story about one partner can surface in searches for the whole practice.

The ethical rules that shape every action

The Italian Bar's code allows lawyers to inform the public about their activity, but the information must be truthful, correct, not misleading and must not compromise dignity and decorum. In practice this sets clear boundaries for professional online reputation management:

  • no disclosure of client names, case details or documents without consent, even when the client has gone public first;
  • no comparative or self-praising claims, and no promises of results;
  • no soliciting clients through intermediaries, unsolicited contact or offers that exploit urgency;
  • no fake or incentivised reviews, which are also banned by Google and by EU consumer law.

Disciplinary proceedings are handled by the district disciplinary councils (Consigli distrettuali di disciplina), and a careless reply to a review is exactly the kind of conduct that can generate a complaint from a former client. Every reputation activity therefore needs to be reviewed through this lens before anything is published.

Answering client reviews without breaching confidentiality

A lawyer can reply to a review, but the reply must never confirm that the reviewer was a client or reveal anything learned during the mandate. Even saying "we represented you in the lease dispute" is a disclosure. The safe response is general, polite and procedural.

A model structure for replies

Thank the person for the feedback, state that professional secrecy prevents discussing any specific matter in public, describe in one sentence how the firm normally works (for example, written fee estimates and regular updates), and invite the reviewer to contact the managing partner directly. This shows prospective clients a calm, professional attitude without entering the merits. Our wider guide on responding to negative reviews without escalation applies here with the additional confidentiality filter.

Reviews written by the opposing party

A frequent problem for litigators is a one-star review from the other side of a case, or from someone the firm never represented. These reviews often breach Google's policies on conflicts of interest and off-topic content, because the author has no client experience to report. They can be flagged through the Business Profile and, if they persist, escalated with the review management tool. The practical steps are described in our article on removing negative Google reviews.

For a lawyer, the best reply to an unfair review is often the most boring one: courteous, brief and silent on the facts. The audience is the next client, not the reviewer.

Collecting genuine feedback within the rules

Reviews from satisfied clients are allowed and useful, provided they are spontaneous and not paid for. The ethical risk lies in the method: offering a fee discount for a review, writing reviews on behalf of clients or asking only happy clients through a filtered process all create problems with both the Bar and Google.

A sustainable approach is to send the same neutral request to every client when a matter is closed, with a direct link to the Business Profile and no suggested wording. Clients in sensitive areas, such as criminal or family law, will often prefer not to leave a public trace; that choice must be respected, and the firm should expect fewer reviews than a dentist or a restaurant. Quality and consistency of the profile, accurate opening hours, practice areas and photos of the office then count more than the number of stars.

Building the firm's and partners' search footprint

Reputation management for professionals rests on owned content that demonstrates competence without advertising results. For a law firm, the most effective assets are informative and verifiable.

AssetWhy it helpsEthical caution
Partner bio pages on the firm siteRank for the lawyer's nameOnly verifiable qualifications
Legal articles and commentaryShow expertise on specific topicsNo references to identifiable cases
LinkedIn profilesStrong ranking for personal namesNo client solicitation in posts
Conference and university pagesIndependent authorityAccurate titles and roles
Bar register and directory listingsOfficial confirmation of standingKeep data consistent everywhere

Consistent naming across these assets, structured data for the firm and each lawyer, and a clear link between partners and the practice help Google show a coherent picture. Medical practices face a similar mix of secrecy duties and patient reviews, as we discuss in our piece on reputation risks for doctors and clinics.

When attacks become defamation or a crisis

Criticism of a lawyer's service is legitimate; false accusations of fraud, collusion or criminal conduct are not. Posts that attribute specific false facts can constitute defamation under art. 595 of the Italian Criminal Code, aggravated when published online, and give grounds for removal requests to platforms under the Digital Services Act as well as civil or criminal action.

Lawyers have an obvious advantage in assessing the legal side, but they are rarely objective about their own case, and filing a complaint against a former client can attract further attention. Preserving evidence with certified screenshots, assessing whether the content is ranking for the firm's name and deciding between removal, delisting and a quiet response is usually best done with an external view.
